title: Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems
summary: Conceptual paper that defines an optimizer by its internal structure (internal search over outputs, policies or plans against an explicitly represented objective), introduces the base optimizer / mesa-optimizer / mesa-objective / behavioral objective vocabulary, and splits alignment into outer alignment (base objective vs intended goal) and inner alignment (mesa-objective vs base objective). Section 2 argues which task and base-optimizer properties make mesa-optimization more likely (environment diversity, pressure toward compressed policies, model capacity, simplicity bias, statefulness; time-complexity penalties and hard-coded search pull the other way). Section 3 describes pseudo-alignment (proxy, approximate and suboptimality alignment) and Section 4 deceptive alignment, giving three conditions for it and arguing that extensive training could end in internalization, corrigible alignment or deception. The paper is explicitly speculative and contains no experiments; it states that current ML systems do not produce dangerous mesa-optimizers and that the lack of a precise definition of optimizer makes it hard to tell whether a model is one.
setting: Theory / conceptual analysis; no models trained. Examples drawn from RL, TreeQN, RL^2, AlphaZero-style search and the evolution analogy.

quotes.quote: We will say that a system is an optimizer if it is internally searching through a search space (consisting of possible outputs, policies, plans, strategies, or similar) looking for those elements that score high according to some objective function that is explicitly represented within the system.
Whether a system is an optimizer is a property of its internal structure—what algorithm it is physically implementing—and not a property of its input-output behavior.

In the context of machine learning, outer alignment refers to aligning the specified loss function with the intended goal, whereas inner alignment refers to aligning the mesa-objective of a mesa-optimizer with the specified loss function.
As one moves to more and more diverse environments—that is, as increases—this model suggests that will dominate , implying that mesa-optimization will become more and more favorable.
Thus, we hypothesize that penalizing description length will favor mesa-optimizers while penalizing time complexity will disfavor them.
The mesa-optimizer must have an objective that extends across parameter updates.
Applying such research to mesa-optimization, however, is hampered by the fact that we currently don’t have a formal specification of optimization.

In this paper, we have argued for the existence of two basic AI safety problems: the problem that mesa-optimizers may arise even when not desired (unintended mesa-optimization), and the problem that mesa-optimizers may not be aligned with the original system’s objective (the inner alignment problem). However, our work is still only speculative.

key_numbers.claim: The paper states current systems do not produce dangerous mesa-optimizers
key_numbers.quote: Certainly, current ML systems do not produce dangerous mesa-optimizers, though whether future systems might is unknown.

key_numbers.claim: Mesa-optimization is expected mainly in more advanced systems; detection is hard without a definition
key_numbers.quote: Moreover, the limited interpretability of neural networks, combined with the fact that there is no general and precise definition of “optimizer,” means that it would be hard to evaluate whether a given model is a mesa-optimizer.

limitations_stated: The authors describe the work as speculative and theoretical; they deliberately give theoretical considerations rather than concrete examples, say an attempt to induce mesa-optimization today would need an artificial setup, and note the absence of a formal specification of optimization. They also flag that it is unclear whether search is necessary or sufficient for coherent objectives.
open_questions: Under what training conditions (task diversity, simplicity vs time-complexity pressure, statefulness) does a learned algorithm become an optimizer? Can an operational definition of optimizer be given so that interpretability can test for it? Does search actually bring a coherent, explicitly represented objective with it?
sense_of_alignment: Alignment between objectives: inner alignment is 'eliminating the base-mesa objective gap', outer alignment is 'eliminating the gap between the base objective and the intended goal of the programmers'.
